stories.title: The Market
stories.fortuneLine: You will trade until the smile owns the barn, and you are only weather sleeping in it.
stories.body:
There was once a man who inherited a great estate: barns of hay, salt for the winters, seed for the spring, strong oxen, and a title to the land itself.

He was a kind man, and no cleverer than kindness required.

When the poor came, he gave. When the merchants came, he smiled and listened.

One day, a trader said, “You have so much hay. Trade it for silk. It will fetch finer coin.” The man agreed.

The silk shimmered. But when storms ruined the fields, his animals, without hay, starved where they stood.

Needing food, he bought meat. But with no salt to preserve it, rot crept into the cellars.

Another trader came and said, “Trade your salt for perfumes. The smell is the problem, not the meat.” And so he did.

The food rotted faster, and his workers fell ill or fled.

When spring came, he had no strong hands to till, and no grain to plant.

Another trader smiled and said, “Trade your seeds for rare spices. Host a grand feast. Call your neighbors. Save your name.” And so he did.

The feast never came. No crops rose. No neighbors answered.

Desperate, he traded his oxen for painted screens, told they would turn his home into a merchant’s hall. The screens cracked in the first autumn wind.

At last, he traded part of his land for gold rings, promised that gold would earn him respect. The merchants took the rings, and the land, and laughed.

When winter fell again, the simpleton stood outside the gates of what had once been his home. The trader lived there now, feasting by firelight.

The trader opened the door and smiled. “You may sleep in the animal barn for one night,” he said, “if you trade me your last thing of value.”

The simpleton looked down at the only thing he still wore: a wool cloak, stitched long ago by his mother’s hands. He handed it over.

And that night, he lay shivering among the oxen, watching the windows of his old home blaze warm against the snow.

No merchant came to trade him back. No friend came to find him. Only the wind. And it asked no price.
